title: Learning in pairs
hookLine: Jews learn two by two, arguing out loud over a text

cards: A library has carpet, quiet, and a sign that says silence please. This room runs the other way. Long tables, and at every table two people bent over one open book, both talking at once.
One jabs a finger at a line. The other shakes her head and flips back a page. Someone laughs.
Someone slaps the table. The noise is a roar, like a train station. That's a Jewish study hall, a beit midrash, on a good day.
Nobody there thinks the noise means nobody's learning. The noise is the learning.

teach.b: The person across the table is your chavruta. It's Aramaic, from chaver, a friend or companion, and it means a study partner and also the partnership itself: you learn in chavruta.
In yeshivas and study halls, this is the usual way to study Torah and Talmud. Not alone with a book. Two people, one text, reading it aloud and arguing about what it says.
The rabbis had a verse from Proverbs: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." The Talmud reads that as two scholars sharpening each other in study.
A blade on a blade makes sparks, and both come away sharper. It goes further. One passage warns that people who study all alone grow foolish, because nobody catches their mistakes.
And there's a story about Honi, the man well-known for drawing a circle and praying for rain. The Talmud says he slept for seventy years, woke, and found nobody who knew him.
He went to the study hall, and nobody believed who he was. He was so lonely that he prayed to die.
The Talmud sums it up with a saying people used: either chavruta, or death. It sounds extreme. The point behind it is plain: in this tradition, people don't just think in their heads.
A partner hears the thing you skipped and asks, where does it say that?
A good chavruta isn't someone who agrees with you. It's someone who cares enough about the text, and about you, to push back. And at the end of the hour, you both close the book as friends.

how: In yeshivas, seminaries and many community study programs, Jews study Torah and Talmud in pairs, reading aloud and debating the text together in a shared study hall.

a teacher who leads a weekly Torah class
a study partner, or learning a text in pairs

games.q: you're in the study hall. your partner reads a line and says it means the opposite of what you think. what does a good chavruta do?
o: nod along to keep the peace.
push back and ask where the text says so.
go find a quieter table and study alone.
games.why: you push back, out loud, and look at the text together. iron sharpens iron: the sparks are the point.

practice: Take one sentence you know, a verse, a proverb, a line a grandparent used to say, and read it slowly in your head. Then let an imaginary partner across the table ask one question: what does that word really mean?
Is that always true? Answer, and let them push back once more.

wordCard.voice: Chavruta. A study partner, from the word for friend: two people, one text, thinking out loud together.

orig.note: Aramaic: a study partnership, from chaver, friend.

carryVoice: Your line: learn with a partner. Iron sharpens iron, and friends close the book together. See you tomorrow.
